@graph.name: Page Data Pool — the Master Database for Page Data
@graph.description: The Page Data Pool is the single master database every page's Page Data dataset draws its slice from — built in two layers. Layer 1 is the estate's own live data: the full intent rubric (3,848 buyer questions with their phrasings, target pages, per-page JSONs and dataset seats), the 32-service registry with its scope-boundary register (18 drafted boundaries, each carrying the ruling it comes from) and its sourced qualifier register (21 qualifiers, each with its source pointer), all 45 dataset files' metadata, the ports matrix (6 ports × 8 offered services with branch bindings), the vault standards registry (UL 608 classes, AA-D-600D classes, FF-L-2740B, UL 768 lock groups), the SIR/KIM-GS authority data (the 1,500–3,500 lb band and the L/360 criterion), the 83-area footprint with branch bindings, the 16-post blog corpus, and the 20-entry audience guide. Layer 2 is a researched domain layer of 45 entries covering the situation space of logistics and every service — container equipment and packing standards (CTU Code, SOLAS VGM), port charges and credentials (FMC demurrage and detention rules, TWIC), export rules (ISPM 15, AES/EEI filing), household-goods consumer law (49 CFR Part 375: binding estimates, the 110% rule, valuation, storage-in-transit), safe and piano data (UL 687/1037/72 classes, IRC floor loads, manufacturer piano weights), and the standards behind the specialty services (ANSI/ESD S20.20, ANSI MH16.1, ASTM D4169/ISTA, NASMM, museum handling practice, EPA electronics rules, carrier delivery tiers, DP3 and FAR Part 47) — every entry carrying its primary or authoritative source, its retrieval date, the questions it answers and its constraints. Layer 2 supplies domain facts only: it never sources a company capability, price, count or credential. The pool also publishes the eleven draw rules (DR-1 to DR-11) by which the generator assembles each page's slice — services, own and family questions, resolved answers, scoped boundaries, traceable qualifiers, drawn domain entries, bound geography and ledger freshness. Buyer-intelligence data is excluded by standing rule, and the false 'industrial rigging up to twenty-five thousand pounds' figure is excluded and asserted absent at build.

Buyer-intelligence data: absent (internal-only standing rule). The 'industrial rigging up to twenty-five thousand pounds' claim: absent — asserted at build; the figure is false and contradicts the SIR band. No USDOT/MC number is carried.

@graph.name: Page Data draw rules — how a page's slice is selected (DR-1 to DR-11)

itemListElement.name: DR-1 Services of the page
itemListElement.description: A page's slice starts from its services: the registry services recorded for the page in data/pages.json, every service whose intent rows target the page, and the page's pageMeta service pointer. A dataset landing draws the service(s) of its dataset file.

itemListElement.name: DR-2 Own questions first
itemListElement.description: The page's question set is every pool question whose targetUrl is the page, clustered by (targetUrl, intentClass, serviceId): the first row of a cluster by rubric id is the canonical question and the remaining rows of the cluster are its alsoAskedAs phrasings. No phrasing is ever duplicated across a page's set.

itemListElement.name: DR-3 Family tier for hubs
itemListElement.description: A hub or guide page additionally draws the family tier: pool questions of the same service(s) whose targetUrl is a sibling page of the same service family, each carrying its own target as evidence. Leaf pages draw their own questions only.

itemListElement.name: DR-4 Answers by resolution, never by invention
itemListElement.description: Each drawn question resolves its answer from the estate at generation time: the target page's per-page JSON FAQPage where the question appears there, else the answer-evidence dataset's fragment for the row. An answer that cannot be resolved from a published seat is not drawn.

itemListElement.name: DR-5 notOffered from the boundary register
itemListElement.description: A page's notOffered set is every boundary-register entry whose scope names one of the page's services, plus every estate-scoped entry, plus any page-scoped entry naming the page. Each entry carries its source into the page's dataset unchanged — the register is the draft set Henry confirms at the rollout, as one consolidated block of the distinct per-service sets; entries are never edited per page.

itemListElement.name: DR-6 Qualifiers by traceability
itemListElement.description: A page may state a qualifier only if it appears in the pool's qualifier register (Layer 1, sourced) or is supported by a Layer-2 domain entry drawn for the page. Every qualifier in a page dataset carries its source pointer. Unsourced qualifiers fail the build (the template lint, PG-3).

itemListElement.name: DR-7 Domain layer draw
itemListElement.description: A page draws the Layer-2 entries whose services intersect the page's services (DR-1). Domain entries supply cited context — standards, regulations, equipment classes, methods — and never company facts: no capability, price, count or credential may be sourced from Layer 2.

itemListElement.name: DR-8 Geography
itemListElement.description: A page's areas are the footprint features whose services include the page's service(s), each with its recorded branch binding (winchester / martinsburg / both). Branch facts are never blended: a page bound to one branch states that branch's name, address and hours only.

itemListElement.name: DR-9 Freshness
itemListElement.description: A page's freshness is the lastmod ledger's date for its URL at generation time; the pool's own dateModified is the ledger date of the pool file.

itemListElement.name: DR-10 Approval
itemListElement.description: ownerApproved rides Henry's adoption of the Page Data header estate-wide (QUEUE-NOTE): the pool is generated from the live estate and Henry's settled rulings, verified by the estate's own gates, and approved per page family at build time — the boundary register's drafts are confirmed by Henry in one block at the rollout.

itemListElement.name: DR-11 Exclusions are structural
itemListElement.description: Buyer-intelligence data never enters the pool (internal-only, standing rule). The 'industrial rigging up to twenty-five thousand pounds' figure never enters: it is false, it contradicts the SIR band, and the pool's build asserts its absence. No USDOT/MC number and no contractor-model explanation is carried — neither is published copy.

itemListElement.description: Data center relocation — the physical layer — from The Flat Rate Movers: servers, populated and de-racked racks and cabinets, storage and network equipment moved between server rooms, colocation facilities and data centers in Northern Virginia and the I-81 corridor as a planned, labelled, documented sequence. The crew performs disconnect and reconnect, de-install and placement — shutdown and unplug in the sequence fixed at survey with the client's IT team, and reconnection, re-cabling and power-up at the destination to the scope agreed at survey; where an element requires certified specialists, the company engages certified contractors for that element. Equipment is inventoried and manifested before anything is unplugged, packed padded, wrapped and strapped with custom crating where needed, sealed with tamper-evident seals, transported in the planned order, and placed in labelled rack and U order, physically verified with the client's team. Retired equipment is packed, sealed, manifested and hauled to the certified ITAD partner engaged for the job; data sanitization, destruction and certification belong to that partner and are never claimed by the company. Populated racks and cabinets in the 1,500–3,500 lb band are surveyed under SIR/KIM-GS with an L/360 floor check. Flat rate quoted in writing before move day. No workload migration or recommissioning is offered or claimed, and the company claims no IT certifications of its own.
itemListElement.source: Henry order 2026-10-30 (work the five takeover categories) + category takeover research 2026-10-30 + owner ruling 2026-10-30 (disconnect/reconnect in scope, performed by the crew; certified contractors engaged for elements requiring certified specialists)

itemListElement.name: Medical & Laboratory Equipment Relocation Logistics
itemListElement.description: Medical and laboratory equipment relocation from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV — hospital, imaging, laboratory and university moves run under SIR (Structural Integrity Relocation) and the KIM-GS Protocol for heavy units of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs with floor deflection analysis to L/360. The full scope is delivered through one engagement: survey and structural check, de-installation and re-installation coordination with the manufacturer's technicians, packing and custom crating, sealed documented transport, placement and leveling, and return-to-service — with calibration, certification, commissioning, decontamination and requalification, and specimen and cold-chain transport, performed by the certified contractors the company engages for that scope, their certifications documented in the bid. Surveyed in full and quoted per job at one flat rate in writing, never by the hour.
itemListElement.source: Henry order 2026-10-30 (work the five takeover categories) + category takeover research 2026-10-30 + transport-only boundary (health-system buyer-intelligence standing rule)

itemListElement.name: Freight Rework & Transloading
itemListElement.description: Freight rework and transloading from Winchester, VA and Martinsburg, WV — shifted loads, loads refused at a receiver's dock, damaged or collapsed pallets, and overweight or axle-illegal loads, unloaded under control, documented as found, rebuilt to the receiver's specification and re-secured to the federal cargo securement standard, plus planned cross-docking and container and rail-to-truck transloading — for drivers, carriers, brokers, 3PLs, warehouses and receivers, quoted at one flat rate before work begins, with emergency and after-hours response available at premium rates. The work is performed where the job requires: leased space, the receiver's dock, or a yard. No rate schedule is published for this service. Quoted flat in writing through the same flat-rate quote path, from Winchester VA and Martinsburg WV.
itemListElement.source: Henry confirmation 2026-11-01 (new category Freight Rework & Transloading: full package treatment) + category research dossier 2026-11-01

itemListElement.name: Vault Door Relocation & Installation
itemListElement.description: Vault Door Relocation & Installation — vault doors and high-security enclosures delivered, relocated, and installed at any size, quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before the job: specified from the door's own standards (UL 608 classes M/1/2/3, GSA Class 5-V / 5-A / 5-B under AA-D-600D, UL 768 lock groups, FF-L-2740B) and its verified weight, planned door by door — rough-opening and swing survey, clear-opening path proof, threshold and step transitions engineered, floor deflection analysis to L/360 inside the SIR 1,500 to 3,500 lb band, setting and leveling to the manufacturer's own installation requirements, contents emptied first, and the combination left in the owner's hands throughout. No locksmith or combination services. Offered from both branches — Winchester VA and Martinsburg WV.

itemListElement.standard: UL 608, Edition 7 (Nov 30, 2004; ANSI reaffirmation Mar 7, 2022, no technical changes) — Burglary Resistant Vault Doors and Modular Panels
itemListElement.attackBasis: Resists attack with common mechanical tools, electric tools, cutting torches, or any combination of these means (UL 608 section 1.2). The attack basis is identical for all four classes; net working time is the only class variable.
itemListElement.exclusions: UL 608 section 1.3: these requirements do not cover attacks with the burning bar (thermal lance) or explosives. No UL 608 class is a rating against explosives or a thermal lance.

itemListElement.name: SIR Method Operations
itemListElement.description: SIR method operations — how a high-mass move is run at The Flat Rate Movers, under SIR (Structural Integrity Relocation) executed through the KIM-GS Protocol, for assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, quoted at one flat rate agreed in writing before move day. The published chain has six steps: (1) the asset — weight, dimensions, centre of mass, and value at risk are established first; (2) the structure — route and clearance survey at both ends, stairs and landings measured, and floor deflection assessed against L/360, span divided by 360, before any lift is planned; (3) the load path — load spreading and protection runs are planned where the substrate needs support, and floors, walls, and frames are protected end to end; (4) the crew and rigging are matched to the plan — dollies, straps, and equipment chosen for this asset and this route; (5) the move — controlled, strapped, and supervised along the planned path; (6) placement — the asset is set in its final position, levelled, and verified with the client, at the flat rate agreed in writing. The structural protocol compresses the same chain into three phases — assess the asset, assess the structure, move under KIM-GS — and calibration-sensitive and fragile high-mass items are flagged at the assess stage, not discovered on the day. The six published steps are the complete published method surface; the protocol's internal calculations, models, and formulas are not published here or anywhere in the company's data. Not published and not claimed: any handling rule below 1,500 lbs or above 3,500 lbs under this method, any equipment beyond the published wording, and any crew-size rule.
itemListElement.source: datasets-sir-heavy.json — carried verbatim

itemListElement.name: Asset & Structure Assessment Operations
itemListElement.description: Asset and structure assessment operations — the survey that gates every SIR move. Published asset inputs: weight, dimensions, centre of mass, and value at risk, with calibration-sensitive and fragile items flagged at the assess stage. Published structure inputs: the route and clearance at both ends, stairs and landings measured, the substrate, and floor deflection assessed against L/360 — span divided by 360 — before any lift is planned; the plan outputs are the load path, the spreading and protection runs, and the crew and rigging matched to the plan. The company's published rule is that the building is assessed before the asset moves: every SIR move starts with the building, not the item. Domain education, labeled as such and never a company figure: L/360 is the standard residential floor deflection limit in the IRC framework (Table R502.3.1) — a 10-foot span may deflect about one-third of an inch, a 12-foot span 0.40 inches, a 15-foot span 0.50 inches — and tile and stone floors demand the stricter L/480. IRC design loads are 40 psf live load in living areas, 30 psf in sleeping areas, and 20 psf in uninhabitable attic storage, plus roughly 10 to 20 psf dead load, all as uniform loads; a heavy asset concentrates its weight on a small footprint, which is why the published method checks the structure first. Not published and not claimed: any PSI value, floor-load figure, or joist schedule as company engineering data, and any involvement of a licensed structural engineer.

itemListElement.name: Vault Door Standards Registry — UL 608, AA-D-600D, FF-L-2740B
itemListElement.description: The verified standards registry for vault doors and high-security enclosures. UL 608 classes M, 1, 2, and 3 carry net working times of 15, 30, 60, and 120 minutes against one identical attack basis — common mechanical tools, electric tools, cutting torches, or any combination — and UL 608 section 1.3 excludes attack with the burning bar (thermal lance) or explosives from every class. GSA Class 5-V under AA-D-600D requires resistance to 20 man-hours of surreptitious entry, 30 man-minutes of covert entry, and 10 man-minutes of forced entry, with no ballistic requirement; Class 5-A drops the surreptitious requirement; Class 5-B adds ballistic resistance tested to SD-STD-01.01 Rev. G level 2, and the specification names no test round. Door lock requirements are recorded as their own fields, never blended into the door figures: Class 5-V and 5-B doors carry a lock meeting FF-L-2740 (Style H or K), while Class 5-A's lock is a UL 768 Group 1 lock. The registry also carries three corrective notes where widely published charts contradict the standards' own text. Every row carries the primary source it was verified against on 2026-11-02.

@graph.name: Layer 1 — the project-type audience guide (five dimensions each)

itemListElement.name: Residential
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Households moving an apartment, townhome or house.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Full-home and partial-home moves, packed or unpacked.
whatToPrepare: Count each room — bedrooms, living rooms, kitchens, bathrooms, home office, garage, basement, loft, patio and any on-property storage.
Note stairs, elevator and parking at both addresses.
List anything unusually heavy or fragile, even if it is under the heavy-asset band.
itemListElement.formFields: Your home — room by room; Full addresses & timing; Access at origin and destination
itemListElement.watchFor: Basements, lofts and sheds hold more than people remember. The room-by-room dropdowns make them visible before the quote is priced.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Local & Regional
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: People and businesses moving inside the Shenandoah Valley and Eastern Panhandle.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Winchester, Martinsburg and the surrounding counties, from either home base.
whatToPrepare: Enter the full city or ZIP for both ends.
Give the date, or say the timing is flexible or a range.
Note parking and any long carry from truck to door.
itemListElement.formFields: Moving from / to; Full addresses & timing; Access — parking at both ends
itemListElement.watchFor: Short distances still fail on access: tight parking and long carries change the crew plan, so they belong in the quote.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Long-Distance
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Households and businesses moving out of the area, with an emphasis on high-value items.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Interstate moves, including heavy or high-value pieces carried under the same standard.
whatToPrepare: Give the destination city or ZIP.
Flag high-value items so protection is planned from the start.
Say whether the delivery timing is fixed, flexible, or a preferred range.
itemListElement.formFields: Moving from / to; Heavy & sensitive items; Services — High-Value Protection; Timing
itemListElement.watchFor: A fixed delivery date and a flexible one plan differently. Say which you have and the quote is built around it.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Senior Moving
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Older adults, families and caregivers managing a downsize or a move to a new home or community.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Downsizing, move-in day, and sorting and packing support.
whatToPrepare: Describe what is staying, going, or being donated.
Say who will be on site to direct the crew.
Record stairs, elevators and parking at both homes.
itemListElement.formFields: Your home — room by room; Services — Packing; Project notes; Video walkthrough
itemListElement.watchFor: The video walkthrough lets family members who live elsewhere show the home without anyone traveling.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Moving & Storage
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Anyone whose move and storage dates do not line up.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Moves into or out of storage — containers, household goods and machines, on a 30-day minimum, with access to your stored items while they are with us.
whatToPrepare: Say what goes to storage and what goes straight to the new address.
Give both dates if you have them — move-out and move-in.
itemListElement.formFields: Project notes / inventory; Full addresses & timing
itemListElement.watchFor: Storage is quoted per job, monthly, or by volume — the notes field is where the split between storage and delivery gets priced correctly.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Junk Removal
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Homeowners and businesses clearing out what is not moving with them.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Removal of furniture, debris and unwanted items as its own job or alongside a move.
whatToPrepare: List what goes and, just as important, what stays.
Note access — stairs, tight doors, long carries.
itemListElement.formFields: What's moving; Project notes / inventory; Access at origin
itemListElement.watchFor: A clear go/stay list is the whole job. Walk the space once with the list in hand before you send the form.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Commercial
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Businesses relocating, expanding or consolidating.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Office and commercial moves, planned around your operation and phased where the job needs it.
whatToPrepare: Give the facility size and the floors involved.
List heavy or sensitive equipment separately from furniture.
Note dock, elevator and parking arrangements at both sites.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy & sensitive items; Access — dock, elevator, parking; Services needed
itemListElement.watchFor: Docks and freight elevators run on building schedules. Put the windows in the notes so the quote plans around them.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Office Moving
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Offices moving desks, files, furniture and equipment.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Whole-office and partial-office relocations.
whatToPrepare: Count workstations and rooms, or give the square footage.
Flag servers, copiers and anything that cannot tilt or stack.
Say whether the move must land outside business hours.
itemListElement.formFields: Full addresses & timing; Heavy & sensitive items; Project notes
itemListElement.watchFor: File rooms and server corners are the two places office quotes go wrong. Name them in the notes even if you estimate.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Industrial Offices
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: The office areas inside plants, warehouses and industrial facilities.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Office relocations planned for the site they sit in — same flat-rate standard, site rules included.
whatToPrepare: Describe the facility and where the office area sits inside it.
Note site rules — check-in, escorts, restricted zones — in the project notes.
List heavy equipment in the office area with weights if known.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy & sensitive items; Access at origin and destination; Project notes
itemListElement.watchFor: An office inside a plant is not a standard office move. The site context is what the crew plan is built from.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Government
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Government offices and agencies moving facilities, offices or equipment.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Agency office moves and equipment relocations, quoted in writing like every job here.
whatToPrepare: Name the facility, the site contact, and any check-in procedure.
List equipment with weights and dimensions where they exist.
Give the required dates — fixed dates are planned as fixed.
itemListElement.formFields: Full addresses & timing; Heavy & sensitive items; Project notes
itemListElement.watchFor: Put the site contact and access procedure in the notes. It is the first thing the crew plan needs and the last thing to leave out.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Military
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Service members, military families and units moving on orders or on their own schedule.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Household and equipment moves tied to reporting dates.
whatToPrepare: Give the reporting or delivery date if it is fixed.
Use the room-by-room section for the household, and the heavy section for safes and equipment.
itemListElement.formFields: Full addresses & timing; Your home — room by room; Heavy & sensitive items
itemListElement.watchFor: Reporting dates do not move. Mark the timing as “must move by” and the quote is planned against it.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Warehouse Relocation
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Warehouses and distribution operations moving sites or reconfiguring.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Warehouse moves, racking moves and load-outs, planned around dock operations.
whatToPrepare: Describe the current and destination layouts, and dock counts.
List racking, machinery and the heaviest pieces with weights if known.
Say what must keep operating during the move.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy & sensitive items; Access — dock at both ends; Project notes
itemListElement.watchFor: What keeps running during the move decides the phasing. State it up front and the quote phases around it.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Data Center & IT
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Data centers and IT operations moving racks, servers and equipment.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Data center and IT relocations, with disconnect and reconnect in scope.
whatToPrepare: List racks and devices, with the heaviest units named.
Note raised floors, dock and elevator specs, and any site access rules in the notes.
Give the maintenance or migration window if there is one.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy & sensitive items; Access at origin and destination; Project notes
itemListElement.watchFor: The window is the job. If there is a fixed migration window, it goes in the timing field, not the small print.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Gun Safes
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Owners of gun safes and vaults, including safes in the 1,500–3,500 lb SIR band.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Gun safe moves — in-home, between addresses, and long-distance — with stairs planned, not improvised.
whatToPrepare: Empty the safe first. The safe is always emptied by the customer before we arrive — firearms and ammunition out.
Give the weight and dimensions if you know them; the make and model help.
Describe stairs, turns and doorways at both ends.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy item chips — Gun safe; Heavy & sensitive items (weight, dimensions); Access — stairs at both ends
itemListElement.watchFor: Weight and stairs decide everything on a safe move. An honest estimate beats a guess — measure the route, not just the safe.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Pianos & Antiques
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Owners of upright and grand pianos, antiques and museum-grade pieces.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Piano and antique moves, protected piece by piece.
whatToPrepare: Name the piece — upright or grand, make if known — and its approximate weight.
Describe stairs, turns and landings at both ends.
Note finishes or fragile points you are worried about in the notes.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy item chips — Piano, Antique / art; Heavy & sensitive items; Access at both ends
itemListElement.watchFor: A grand is dismantled onto a padded skid board; an upright travels secured on a dolly or skid. The route decides which plan the quote carries.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Medical Equipment
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Clinics, labs and practices moving medical devices and equipment.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Medical equipment relocation, from single devices to full rooms.
whatToPrepare: List each device with its weight if known.
Note floor type and any level changes on the route.
Say whether the equipment must be running again by a fixed time.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy item chips — Medical; Heavy & sensitive items; Access — floor type at both ends
itemListElement.watchFor: Heavy devices are planned with a floor-deflection check before anything lifts. The floor type fields are there for exactly this.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.name: Cryogenic
itemListElement.whoItIsFor: Labs and facilities moving cryogenic units and freezers.
itemListElement.jobsItCovers: Cryogenic equipment moves, planned as heavy, sensitive items.
whatToPrepare: Name the unit and its weight if known.
Note anything that must stay upright or powered, in the project notes.
Describe access at both ends — docks, elevators, floor type.
itemListElement.formFields: Heavy item chips — Cryogenic; Heavy & sensitive items; Access at both ends
itemListElement.watchFor: What the unit cannot do — tilt, wait, warm up — belongs in the notes. The quote plans around the constraint, not around the average case.
itemListElement.source: datasets-quote-tool.json — the 20-audience guide (content_data.py, the live page's generator source)

itemListElement.headline: Container packing — the CTU Code
itemListElement.name: L2-CTU-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The IMO/ILO/UNECE Code of Practice for Packing of Cargo Transport Units (the CTU Code, 2014) is the global reference for how cargo is packed and secured in containers and other cargo transport units; it gives advice to the packer, the parties in the supply chain, and those who unpack the unit. The Code is non-mandatory and does not replace national or international regulations that apply to a single transport mode. It addresses the failure modes behind most container incidents: inadequate securing, overloading, and incorrect declaration of contents. It assigns the packing duties to the packer — fitness of the unit, distribution, securing, segregation, closure, marks and the packing certificate — while terminal, carrier and ship checks at acceptance are external only: a sealed unit is not opened to verify its interior.

Is the CTU Code a law or a code of practice?
constraints: The CTU Code is guidance, not a regulation in itself; binding rules (IMDG for dangerous goods, SOLAS VGM) sit alongside it.
A carrier's external acceptance check never certifies the interior packing — the packer's certificate does.

itemListElement.headline: Container packing — tight stow vs secured stow, load distribution
itemListElement.name: L2-CTU-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Under the CTU Code's packing annex, a load is planned as either a tight stow — packages placed tightly within the walls of the unit — or a secured stow, where packages that do not fill the space are restrained by blocking and/or lashing; in both cases the load is distributed evenly across the container floor. Planning happens before packing starts: fitness of the unit is verified first, package compatibility is checked, and moisture-sensitive cargo is never packed with wet cargo, leaking cargo or wet timber dunnage. Damaged packages are not packed unless precautions are taken against spillage. Dunnage, friction-increasing material and lashings are selected as part of the plan, and wood dunnage must respect quarantine (ISPM 15) rules.

itemListElement.headline: Container equipment — 20 ft standard dry container
itemListElement.name: L2-EQP-01
itemListElement.articleBody: A 20 ft standard dry container measures 5,896 mm long × 2,350 mm wide × 2,393 mm high inside, with a door opening of about 2,339 mm wide × 2,274 mm high; maximum gross mass 30,480 kg, tare about 2,280 kg, maximum payload about 28,200 kg, capacity about 33 m³. Maersk Line's equipment guide figures. The door opening — not the internal dimensions — is the binding constraint for a single large piece: a crate can fit the interior and still fail at the door. Dense cargo suits the 20 ft unit because its payload-to-volume ratio is the highest of the standard dry fleet.

itemListElement.headline: Container equipment — 40 ft standard and 40 ft high-cube
itemListElement.name: L2-EQP-02
itemListElement.articleBody: A 40 ft standard dry container measures 12,032 mm long × 2,350 mm wide × 2,393 mm high inside (about 67 m³, max payload about 28,800 kg, tare about 3,700 kg); a 40 ft high-cube raises internal height to 2,697 mm and the door opening to about 2,577 mm high (about 76 m³, max payload about 28,620 kg). Maersk Line's equipment guide figures. Because the 40 ft units share the 20 ft unit's gross-mass class, the longer box trades payload for volume: light, bulky cargo cubes out a 40 ft before it weighs out, while dense cargo reaches the payload ceiling of a 40 ft with space left over — the standard reason dense freight is planned into 20 ft units and voluminous freight into 40 ft or high-cube units.

itemListElement.headline: SOLAS verified gross mass (VGM)
itemListElement.name: L2-VGM-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Since 1 July 2016, SOLAS Chapter VI Regulation 2 requires the shipper named on the bill of lading to provide the verified gross mass (VGM) of every packed container — the total of cargo, pallets, dunnage, securing material and the container's tare — before loading; a container without a VGM is not loaded. Exactly two methods are permitted: Method 1, weighing the packed, sealed container; or Method 2, weighing all cargo items and adding the container's tare mass as shown on its door. The VGM travels in a signed shipping document to the master and the terminal in time for the stowage plan; carrier and terminal cut-offs are commercial deadlines set per port call, not by SOLAS itself. A packing-list total or a booking estimate is not a VGM.

itemListElement.headline: VGM in the United States — Coast Guard equivalence
itemListElement.name: L2-VGM-02
itemListElement.articleBody: On 28 April 2016 the U.S. Coast Guard declared the existing U.S. laws and regulations for providing verified container weights equivalent to SOLAS VI/2, so U.S. export shippers may work through arrangements in which a terminal verifies the VGM for an authorizing shipper, or the shipper verifies the cargo while the carrier verifies the tare. The equivalence finding is about who may produce the number, not about whether it is needed: the verified weight still has to reach the master before loading, and the shipper's responsibility is unchanged.

itemListElement.headline: Demurrage and detention — what the charges are
itemListElement.name: L2-FMC-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Demurrage is the charge for keeping a container inside the terminal beyond the free time the tariff allows; detention (per diem) is the charge for keeping the container outside the terminal — on the street, at a warehouse — beyond free time. Both are per-container, per-day charges assessed under the carrier's or terminal's tariff. The Federal Maritime Commission's interpretive rule (46 CFR 545.5) frames both charges by their incentive purpose: they exist to promote freight fluidity — cargo and equipment moving, not sitting. Free time, the charge clock, and when the clock stops are tariff questions, answered in the carrier's or marine terminal operator's published tariff for the specific port.

itemListElement.headline: Demurrage and detention billing — the 2024 rule and its current status
itemListElement.name: L2-FMC-02
itemListElement.articleBody: The FMC's Demurrage and Detention Billing Requirements (46 CFR Part 541, effective 28 May 2024 under the Ocean Shipping Reform Act of 2022) require invoices to carry accurate, complete information and to be issued within 30 days; an invoice that fails those requirements eliminates the billed party's obligation to pay. On 23 September 2025 the D.C. Circuit vacated only §541.4 — the provision limiting who may be invoiced — and the rest of the rule remains in force. Practical consequence for cargo owners working a port problem: the invoice-content and 30-day rules are live law, disputes run through the billing party's dispute process and the FMC's complaint and assistance channels, and who may lawfully be billed for a given charge is the one question the court sent back — it is answered case by case, not by the vacated list.

itemListElement.headline: TWIC — who needs the credential at a port
itemListElement.name: L2-TWIC-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The Transportation Worker Identification Credential (TWIC) is required by the Maritime Transportation Security Act for workers who need unescorted access to secure areas of the nation's maritime facilities and vessels; TSA runs the security threat assessment and issues the biometric credential, the U.S. Coast Guard governs how facilities use it at the gate, and the card is valid for five years. Holders include longshore and terminal staff, truck drivers picking up or delivering inside terminals, merchant mariners with Coast Guard credentials, and contractors, surveyors and repair crews working inside secure areas. A worker without a TWIC can only enter escorted. TSA recommends enrolling at least 60 days before the credential is needed; processing can exceed 45 days.

itemListElement.headline: ISPM 15 — approved treatments and their parameters
itemListElement.name: L2-ISPM-01
itemListElement.articleBody: ISPM 15, the IPPC (FAO) standard for wood packaging material in international trade, approves heat treatment (HT — wood core held at a minimum of 56 °C for at least 30 minutes), dielectric heating (DH — 60 °C for 1 minute), methyl bromide fumigation (MB) and sulfuryl fluoride (SF); the wood must be debarked, and treated material carries the IPPC mark. The standard exists to stop wood-boring pests moving between countries in pallets, crates and dunnage. Methyl bromide is banned in the EU and restricted elsewhere, and MB-treated U.S. wood packaging is not accepted by the EU or China — heat treatment is the default compliant route for U.S. export work. Treatment must happen before the packaging is packed into a container; in-situ treatment is not permitted.

itemListElement.headline: ISPM 15 — reading the mark, and U.S. enforcement
itemListElement.name: L2-ISPM-02
itemListElement.articleBody: The ISPM 15 mark carries four elements — the IPPC symbol, the two-letter country code, the unique facility number assigned under the national program, and the treatment code (HT or MB) — and since 1 January 2026 U.S. enforcement again requires the hyphen between the country code and the facility number; wood packaging entering the United States must be pest-free, debarked, treated and marked, or the shipment is refused entry. USDA APHIS administers the U.S. import rule and the American Lumber Standard Committee (ALSC) program accredits the facilities that may apply the mark. Inspectors look for the official mark and for any sign of pests; agricultural inspectors can issue an Emergency Action Notification for noncompliant wood packaging, and cargo can be held, separated from its packaging for re-export, or refused outright, with CBP penalties possible under Title 19.

itemListElement.headline: ISPM 15 — what is exempt
itemListElement.name: L2-ISPM-03
itemListElement.articleBody: ISPM 15 does not apply to packaging made entirely of processed wood — plywood, particle board, veneer and similar material manufactured with glue, heat or pressure — nor to wood shavings, sawdust, wood wool, or wood thinner than 6 mm. The exemption turns on the material, not the shipment: a crate framed in solid timber with plywood panels is regulated for its solid-wood parts, and solid-wood dunnage inside a container is regulated even when the cargo itself is not wood. Domestic U.S. moves are outside the standard entirely — ISPM 15 governs international trade — and U.S.–Canada movement of U.S./Canadian-origin wood packaging is exempt under 7 CFR 319.40-3, while Mexico requires full ISPM 15 compliance.

itemListElement.headline: Export filing — EEI/AES and the $2,500 line
itemListElement.name: L2-EXP-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Under the Foreign Trade Regulations (15 CFR Part 30), Electronic Export Information must be filed through the Automated Export System (AES, inside CBP's ACE platform) whenever the goods under a single Schedule B number, from one exporter to one consignee on one conveyance, exceed $2,500 — and at any value when the shipment requires an export license; a successful filing returns an Internal Transaction Number (ITN) that travels with the shipment. The threshold is per classification line, not per invoice total: five lines of $600 each do not trigger filing, one line of $2,600 does. The U.S. Principal Party in Interest (USPPI) owns the filing duty; exporters file free through AESDirect with an IRS-issued EIN and an ACE exporter account. Shipments to Canada are generally exempt (with exceptions, including used self-propelled vehicles, which always require filing).

itemListElement.headline: The Port of Virginia — terminals and inland reach
itemListElement.name: L2-PORT-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The Port of Virginia, owned by the Virginia Port Authority, operates four Hampton Roads marine terminals — Norfolk International Terminals, Virginia International Gateway, Portsmouth Marine Terminal and Newport News Marine Terminal — plus two inland facilities: the Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, an intermodal container transfer facility at the I-66/I-81 junction that receives containers by rail from the coast, and the Richmond Marine Terminal on the James River, linked to Norfolk Harbor by container-on-barge service. Norfolk Harbor is the deepest harbor on the U.S. East Coast (50 ft, authorized to 55 ft), and NIT and VIG both offer on-dock double-stack rail with CSX and Norfolk Southern. The Virginia Inland Port — the first inland port established in the United States — puts the port's gate 220 highway miles inland, inside the Shenandoah Valley's distribution cluster, which is why Valley warehouses treat Front Royal as their port terminal.

itemListElement.headline: Transloading — what it is, and how it differs from cross-docking and drayage
itemListElement.name: L2-TRN-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Transloading is the physical transfer of freight itself from one transport unit or mode to another at an intermediate facility — classically, unloading an ocean container and reloading its cargo into domestic trailers or rail equipment. It is distinct from cross-docking (inbound freight moved straight to outbound vehicles with minimal storage and no repacking), from intermodal transfer (a sealed container changes mode without being opened), and from drayage (the short truck haul that moves the container between the terminal and the facility). A typical transload runs five stages: receipt and document verification, unloading with count and condition inspection, the mode/equipment transfer, value-added handling (palletizing, labeling, kitting, repacking), and dispatch. Importers transload to convert 40 ft ocean equipment into 53 ft domestic trailers, to split or consolidate loads, and to break heavyweight ocean loads into legal-weight domestic trailers.

itemListElement.headline: Safe ratings — UL 687 tool-resistant classes (TL-15, TL-30)
itemListElement.name: L2-SAFE-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Under UL 687, the U.S. standard for burglary-resistant safes, a TL-15 safe has resisted expert attack with common hand and power tools for 15 minutes of net working time, and a TL-30 for 30 minutes; net working time counts only while a tool is actually on the safe, and a TL rating's test attack is directed at the door and front face unless the rating carries the X6 suffix. TL-15 construction requires the equivalent of 1-inch solid steel in the tested construction. The rating ladder continues TL-30x6 (30 minutes on all six sides), then the torch classes. A safe's rating is a property of the tested model — it appears on the label inside the door — and it describes attack resistance, not weight: two safes with the same rating can differ by hundreds of pounds, which is why a move is planned from the safe's actual weight and path, not its rating.

itemListElement.headline: Safe ratings — torch and explosive classes (TRTL, TXTL), and EN 1143-1
itemListElement.name: L2-SAFE-02
itemListElement.articleBody: UL 687's upper classes add attack types: TRTL ratings (e.g., TRTL-30) certify resistance to cutting torches as well as tools for the stated minutes, and TXTL-60 certifies 60 minutes against torch, tools and explosives. Europe grades safes under EN 1143-1 (Grades 0–XIII by resistance units) and secure cabinets under EN 14450 (S1/S2) — a European grade and a UL class are different test systems and do not convert into each other. For a move, the rating's practical content is handling: torch-class and high-grade safes concentrate mass in door and body construction, and their locks (UL 768 combination locks, UL 887 time locks) are the components a relocation must never shock, tilt beyond maker limits, or expose to combination changes by unqualified hands.

itemListElement.headline: Safe ratings — RSC (UL 1037) and fire classes (UL 72)
itemListElement.name: L2-SAFE-03
itemListElement.articleBody: Most residential gun safes carry no UL 687 rating at all; the residential scale is UL 1037's Residential Security Container (RSC) ladder — RSC I resists 5 minutes of manual-tool attack, RSC II 10 minutes including power tools, RSC III heavier tools with a smaller permitted opening. Fire protection is a separate UL 72 scale stated as an interior-temperature class: Class 350 (paper), Class 150 and Class 125 (media and data). A safe advertised as 'fireproof' with no UL 72 class, and a gun safe with no RSC or TL label, are un-rated products whatever their steel gauge — the label inside the door is the only evidence. For relocation planning the rating still matters less than the scale weight: residential gun safes commonly run from a few hundred pounds to well over 1,500 lb in the largest RSC cabinets.

itemListElement.headline: Residential floors — design live loads (IRC Table R301.5)
itemListElement.name: L2-FLOOR-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The International Residential Code designs one- and two-family dwelling floors for a minimum uniformly distributed live load of 40 pounds per square foot in rooms other than sleeping rooms, 30 psf in sleeping rooms and habitable attics, and 40 psf on stairs — with individual stair treads also checked against a 300-pound concentrated load. These are uniform-load design values for the floor system as a whole, not a promise about any single point: a heavy safe or piano delivers its weight through a small footprint, so the planning question is the concentrated load on the joists below and how it is spread — the reason heavy-piece placements are checked against the structure (span, joist size, bearing walls) rather than against the room's psf number alone. IRC Table R301.7 separately caps floor-member deflection at L/360 under live load.

itemListElement.headline: Piano weights — manufacturer specifications (Steinway)
itemListElement.name: L2-PIANO-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Steinway & Sons publishes its grand piano range at 540 lb for the 5 ft 1 in Model S up to 990 lb (480 kg) for the 8 ft 11¾ in concert grand Model D, with the widely owned Model B (6 ft 11 in) at 760 lb (345 kg); the same maker's string tension runs from about 39,000 lb on a Model B to about 45,400 lb on a Model D. Manufacturer-published figures — the planning inputs for a piano move are the model's published weight and length, the leg/pedal-lyre removal the design allows, and the path (a grand travels on its side on a piano board, so door height and turn radii are measured against the piano's length, not its footprint). Uprights concentrate similar mass in a tall, narrow case that tips rather than slides, which is why upright and grand technique differ.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — binding vs non-binding estimates (49 CFR 375.403)
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-01
itemListElement.articleBody: For an interstate household-goods move, federal law (49 CFR Part 375) requires a written estimate based on a physical survey of the goods, stating whether it is binding or non-binding: a binding estimate guarantees the total cost for the quantities and services shown, whatever the shipment finally weighs; a non-binding estimate is an approximation, with final charges set by the actual weight and services. A verbal quote is not an estimate under the rule. If a shipper adds services after a binding estimate is signed, the carrier issues a revised binding estimate rather than repricing at delivery. The estimate must also state the shipper's two liability options — Full Value Protection, or waiver to Released Value — before the move is booked.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — the 110% rule at delivery
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-02
itemListElement.articleBody: On a non-binding estimate, a mover may not demand more than 110% of the estimated amount at delivery (plus charges for extra services the shipper requested after contracting, and capped impracticable-operations charges); the mover must relinquish the shipment on payment of that amount and bill any remaining balance no sooner than 30 days after delivery. The rule is the federal answer to the hostage load: refusal to release a shipment after the shipper tenders 110% of a non-binding estimate violates Part 375. Impracticable-operations charges collected at delivery are themselves capped at 15% of all other charges due at delivery, with the rest billed afterward.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — valuation: Full Value Protection vs Released Value
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-03
itemListElement.articleBody: Federal law requires an interstate mover to offer two liability levels: Full Value Protection, under which the mover repairs, replaces, or pays the current market value of a lost or damaged article; and Released Value, the no-extra-charge default if the shipper waives Full Value Protection in writing, which limits recovery to 60 cents per pound per article regardless of the article's value. Valuation is the mover's contractual liability limit, not an insurance policy — separate third-party insurance is a different product. The arithmetic is unforgiving: under Released Value a 50 lb television lost outright pays at most $30. The shipper's choice must appear on the estimate, and a mover may set minimum valuation levels and deductibles under Full Value Protection in its tariff.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — the Rights and Responsibilities booklet and the physical survey
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-04

itemListElement.headline: Storage-in-transit (SIT) — conversion and notice (49 CFR 375.609)
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-05
itemListElement.articleBody: When household goods are held in storage-in-transit under an interstate move, the carrier must notify the shipper in writing at least 10 days before the SIT period expires, stating the date the goods convert to permanent storage, that the carrier's liability then ends and the warehouseman's rules and charges take over, and that the shipper has a 9-month window after conversion to claim for loss or damage from the transit/SIT period; if the carrier fails to notify, its carrier liability continues until the day after notice is actually given. There is no single federal number of SIT days: the period is the one specified for the shipment or the maximum in the carrier's tariff. SIT is legally a continuation of the move — carrier liability, valuation and claim rights ride with the goods — while permanent storage is a warehouse relationship; the conversion notice is the moment one legal regime hands over to the other, which is why the regulation polices it.

itemListElement.headline: Claims — the Carmack framework (49 U.S.C. 14706)
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-06
itemListElement.articleBody: Loss-and-damage claims against an interstate household-goods carrier run under the Carmack Amendment framework (49 U.S.C. 14706): the carrier is liable for actual loss or damage to the shipment while in its custody, the shipper files a written claim (the Part 375 window is 9 months), and FMCSA itself has no authority to order a carrier to pay a claim — disputed claims resolve through the carrier's federally required arbitration program or in court. FMCSA's consumer guidance is explicit that the agency regulates and can act against a carrier's authority, but payment of an individual claim is a matter between shipper, carrier, arbitration and the courts. Keeping the bill of lading, the estimate, the inventory and delivery paperwork is what makes a claim provable.

itemListElement.headline: Brokers vs carriers — who actually moves the goods
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-07
itemListElement.articleBody: A household-goods broker arranges transportation but does not itself transport; under 49 CFR 375.409 a broker may give an estimate only where a written agreement makes that estimate the estimate of the authorized motor carrier that will actually perform the move, and the carrier remains bound by every Part 375 duty, including relinquishing the shipment at 110% of a non-binding estimate. The practical test is identity: the name on the bill of lading and the U.S. DOT number behind it belong to the carrier answerable for the shipment. A deposit paid to a broker does not change who carries the goods or who owes the delivery duties.

itemListElement.headline: West Virginia intrastate moves — PSC certificate
itemListElement.name: L2-STATE-01
itemListElement.articleBody: A carrier transporting household goods for hire within West Virginia must hold operating authority — a certificate of convenience and necessity — issued by the West Virginia Public Service Commission under W. Va. Code §24A-2-5; operating without it is a violation the PSC enforces, and the carrier's rates and practices sit inside its filed PSC authority. itemListElement.headline: Government freight — FAR Part 47 and rate tenders
itemListElement.name: L2-GOV-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Federal agencies acquire transportation and transportation-related services (including storage, packing and marking) under FAR Part 47 or under the government rate-tender statutes (49 U.S.C. 10721 and 13712); domestic shipments move on commercial bills of lading, government bills of lading are used for international and noncontiguous domestic shipments when authorized, and documentation, payment and audit for civilian agencies run under 41 CFR Part 102-118 (for DoD, the Defense Transportation Regulation, DoD 4500.9-R). Household goods for the government are carved out of FAR Part 47's contract procedures — HHG rates are established under the 10721/13712 tender system instead — which is why military personal-property moves run on tenders of service rather than FAR freight contracts.

itemListElement.headline: Military moves — the DP3 Tender of Service program
itemListElement.name: L2-MIL-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Military household-goods moves run through USTRANSCOM's Defense Personal Property Program (DP3): carriers participate as approved Transportation Service Providers under the DP3 Household Goods Tender of Service (the 2026 ToS is managed by the Defense Personal Property Management Office at Scott AFB), rates sit in the 400NG tariff framework, and shipment weights for tender purposes are estimated at seven pounds per cubic foot for items not covered by the program's weight estimator. In October 2025 the Department terminated the replacement Global Household Goods Contract for cause and directed that the Tender of Service program be retained and modernized for a minimum of three years — so the ToS, not the GHC, is the operative program a military family or a servicing mover deals with. Personally Procured Moves (PPM) are the self-move alternative reimbursed against the government's constructed cost.

itemListElement.headline: Packaging performance testing — ASTM D4169
itemListElement.name: L2-PACK-01
itemListElement.articleBody: ASTM D4169 is the standard practice for performance testing of shipping containers and systems: a package or crate design is subjected to a laboratory test plan built from a distribution cycle (DC) that mirrors its real journey — handling drops and impacts, compression under stacking, vehicle and loose-load vibration, and environmental hazards — at a chosen assurance level. The cycles are specific: DC 3 is the single-package environment up to 100 lb, DC 4 covers motor-freight single packages over 100 lb, DC 6 motor freight unitized, DC 10 rail-and-motor unitized, and so on. For custom crating the practice is the engineering reference for 'how much protection is enough': the crate is designed against the hazards of its actual distribution cycle rather than against a generic drop height.

itemListElement.headline: Unitized loads — ISTA 3E and the IoPP freight guide
itemListElement.name: L2-PACK-02
itemListElement.articleBody: ISTA Procedure 3E is the general-simulation test for unitized loads — products secured together on a skid or pallet and distributed as a single load — running atmospheric conditioning, incline impact, rotational edge drops, compression and random vibration in sequence. The Institute of Packaging Professionals' freight guide treats shipments of 151 lb and over, and unitized or palletized freight generally, as the freight-packaging design class, recommending preshipment testing under ISTA 3E or ASTM D4169 cycles 4–12. The unitized-load idea governs most commercial freight handling: once freight is palletized and restrained as one unit, every handler downstream treats it as one object — which is why restraint (stretch wrap, banding, corner protection) is part of the packaging design and not an afterthought at the dock.

itemListElement.headline: ESD control — ANSI/ESD S20.20 program standard
itemListElement.name: L2-DC-01
itemListElement.articleBody: ANSI/ESD S20.20-2021 is the standard for an electrostatic-discharge control program protecting electrical and electronic parts, assemblies and equipment susceptible to discharges of 100 volts human-body-model and 200 volts charged-device-model and above; it applies expressly to organizations that transport or otherwise handle such items, on three principles: all conductors (including personnel) bonded to ground, charge on essential insulators controlled, and ESD-sensitive items transported outside a protected area only in static-protective enclosures. The standard's transport rule is the one that reaches a relocation: inside an ESD Protected Area, grounded handling governs; the moment a server, board or instrument leaves the EPA, it travels enclosed in protective materials. Damage from ESD is frequently latent — a device can pass a power-on check and fail early in service — which is why handling discipline, not post-move testing, is the control.

itemListElement.headline: Dry ice transport — 49 CFR 173.217 (UN 1845)
itemListElement.name: L2-MED-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Dry ice (carbon dioxide, solid, UN 1845, Class 9) used as a refrigerant must travel in packaging designed to vent the gas so pressure cannot rupture it; by air, each package is marked 'Carbon dioxide, solid' or 'Dry ice' with the net mass of dry ice shown, the shipper must arrange the shipment with the operator, and the IATA limit is 200 kg of dry ice per package — while a package containing no more than 2.5 kg used as a refrigerant qualifies for the regulation's exception when marked as required. The modal split surprises people: under 49 CFR 173.217 dry ice is regulated when offered by aircraft or vessel, and the section sets no requirements for highway or rail — the same shipper box that is unregulated on a truck becomes a documented hazardous-material package the moment it is tendered to an airline. By vessel, packages carry 'CARBON DIOXIDE, SOLID — DO NOT STOW BELOW DECKS' and freight containers are placarded on two sides.

itemListElement.headline: Liquid nitrogen — properties and the oxygen-displacement hazard
itemListElement.name: L2-MED-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Liquid nitrogen boils at −195.8 °C and expands about 696 times in volume when it vaporizes; the gas is inert, colorless and odorless with no warning properties, and released in a confined space it displaces oxygen — OSHA sets 19.5% oxygen as the minimum concentration for work without supplied-air respiratory protection, and areas using liquid nitrogen require ventilation (a minimum of six air changes per hour is the published EHS benchmark) and, where displacement is possible, oxygen monitoring. Cryogenic equipment travels in the containers built for it — dewars, cryogenic liquid cylinders (insulated, vacuum-jacketed pressure vessels) and storage tanks — never in improvised sealed vessels: a closed container of cryogen is a pressure rupture waiting for time. Cold contact causes severe frostbite; handling uses loose-fitting insulated cryogenic gloves and eye protection. These properties — not the weight alone — are what make a cryogenic freezer or dewar a planned move: route, ventilation of the vehicle and the destination room, and the vessel's own relief devices are checked before anything lifts.

itemListElement.headline: Industrial racking — ANSI MH16.1 (RMI)
itemListElement.name: L2-WH-01
itemListElement.articleBody: ANSI MH16.1-2023, the Rack Manufacturers Institute standard referenced by the International Building Code, governs the design, testing and utilization of industrial steel storage racks — pallet, pallet-flow, push-back, case-flow racks, pick modules and rack-supported systems — including the rule that all rack columns are anchored to the floor with bolts on base plates, and that each installation carries load plaques stating its rated configuration (the Load Application and Rack Configuration, LARC). MH16.1 does not cover cantilever rack (ANSI MH16.3), drive-in/drive-through or portable racks. The relocation consequence: a rack system's rating belongs to its engineered configuration — beam levels, anchors, base plates and the slab it stands on — so a rack moved and re-erected in a different configuration is a new installation to be configured and plaqued, not the old rating carried over.

itemListElement.headline: Senior move management — the NASMM model and ethics code
itemListElement.name: L2-SEN-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The National Association of Senior & Specialty Move Managers (NASMM, founded 2002) is the membership body for Senior Move Managers: practitioners who manage the whole transition for older adults — an overall move or age-in-place plan, organizing, sorting and downsizing, customized floor plans for the new home, arranging disposal of unwanted items through auction, estate sale, consignment or donation, and coordinating the move itself — under a signed Code of Ethics whose first standards are advocacy and loyalty to the person in transition, respect for the client's self-determination, and privacy. NASMM general members complete its Cornerstone Course program, carry liability insurance, and submit to Ethics Compliance Commission oversight; 'Senior Move Manager' is a registered service mark only members may use. The model's distinction from a moving crew is scope: the manager owns the decisions-and-dispersal project around the physical move, which is the part of a late-life relocation that actually takes the weeks.

itemListElement.headline: Museum object handling — preventive-conservation practice
itemListElement.name: L2-MUS-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Published museum object-handling procedure treats every object as irreplaceable: handle only when necessary; know the object's condition before touching it; never lift by protruding handles, rims or other structurally weak parts; support fragile objects on a tray or mount before lifting; move one object at a time (small items together only in a padded, separated tray); never layer or stack objects in transit; and wear appropriate gloves with clean hands to keep salts and oils off surfaces. Before any move, the handler evaluates the object's structure, prior repairs and documented hazards, and checks catalog records, condition reports and photographs — an object that is not stable is not moved until a collections specialist clears it. Damage, when it happens, is reported and recorded in the catalog record immediately; the record-keeping is part of the handling standard, not paperwork after it.

itemListElement.headline: Condition reports — the museum loan/move record
itemListElement.name: L2-MUS-02
itemListElement.articleBody: A museum condition report documents an object's condition on a specific date — overall condition term (Excellent / Good / Fair / Poor, from like-new through unstable), a narrative that summarizes first and details after, the location of any damage described against landmarks on the object (proper left, upper left, reverse), and material-specific damage notes — and it is re-made at each custody change so change over time is provable. The Smithsonian's own collection-move specification builds this into contract scope: the mover creates condition records during the move, rehousing objects into archival-quality material sized for transport, under institutional supervision, with fine-arts rigging by a qualified rigger for large objects. For loans, Smithsonian Affiliations policy requires borrowers to care for objects to American Alliance of Museums standards and to provide regular condition reports during the loan.

itemListElement.headline: Electronics disposal — EPA's framework (CRT rule, household exclusion, certified recyclers)
itemListElement.name: L2-JUNK-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Under EPA's RCRA framework, used cathode-ray tubes and CRT glass being recycled are conditionally excluded from hazardous-waste regulation when the CRT rule's conditions are met (40 CFR 261.4(a)(22)); electronics discarded by households are household hazardous waste, exempt from federal hazardous-waste rules (40 CFR 261.4(b)(1)); and EPA directs debris managers to certified electronics recyclers — the two accredited standards are the R2 (Responsible Recycling) standard and the e-Stewards standard. Older televisions and monitors carry an average of about four pounds of lead in the tube, which is why the CRT stream is regulated at all. The practical sorting rule for a cleanout: working electronics go to donation/reuse first (reuse sits above recycling in EPA's waste hierarchy), non-working electronics go to a certified recycler or a local household-hazardous-waste program, and lithium-ion batteries never go in household garbage or curbside recycling — they go to dedicated battery collection with terminals protected.

itemListElement.headline: Delivery service tiers — curbside, threshold, room of choice, white glove
itemListElement.name: L2-WG-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The last-mile industry names four ascending service levels: curbside/doorstep (the item is left outside the door), threshold (carried just inside the first dry covered area — entryway, garage, lobby), room of choice (carried to the room the customer names, left boxed, no assembly), and white glove (room-of-choice placement plus unpacking, light assembly or setup, inspection with the crew present, and removal of all packaging and debris). The tier names are carrier-published service definitions, not a single regulated standard — providers scope them slightly differently, so the operative questions at booking are where the item stops, whether unpacking/assembly is in, and whether packaging leaves with the crew. Stairs change the tier math: threshold crews stop at the entry level by definition, so an upstairs room requires room-of-choice or white glove scope regardless of the item.

itemListElement.headline: White glove — what a properly scoped job includes
itemListElement.name: L2-WG-02
itemListElement.articleBody: A properly scoped white-glove delivery is built around a scheduled appointment window with pre-delivery contact, a two-person crew with handling gear (straps, blankets, floor protection), carry-in including stairs to the named room, uncrating and basic assembly, placement to the customer's floor plan, and photo-documented completion with all packaging removed. itemListElement.headline: Corridor geography — the I-81/I-66 junction and the inland port
itemListElement.name: L2-COR-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The Virginia Inland Port sits at Front Royal where I-66 meets I-81, 220 miles inland from the Hampton Roads terminals; containers move between the coast and Front Royal by rail, and the terminal serves markets across Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, Ohio and the Washington, D.C. region — making the northern Shenandoah Valley a working extension of the port rather than a remote delivery zone. I-81 is the Valley's north–south freight spine and I-66 its east–west link to the capital region; the junction is why distribution square footage clusters in the Winchester–Front Royal corridor (the VEDP account counts some 240 warehouse and distribution centers, roughly 60 million square feet, using the Port of Virginia statewide).

itemListElement.headline: UL 608 — net working time is the rating
itemListElement.name: L2-VAULT-01
itemListElement.articleBody: UL 608 rates burglary-resistant vault doors by net working time: the minutes of actual attack the door withstands, on one identical attack basis for every class — Class M 15 minutes, Class 1 30 minutes, Class 2 60 minutes, Class 3 120 minutes. Net working time counts only the time the attack tools are working on the door; it is the figure the classes are built on, and the four classes differ in minutes alone, not in the kind of attack. The standard's own scope (section 1.3) excludes attacks using a burning bar or explosives, so no UL 608 class is a rating against those methods, whatever secondary charts imply. A door described as 'built to UL 608' without the UL Mark has not been through UL's certification and follow-up surveillance; the class claim and the certification are different things.

itemListElement.headline: GSA Class 5 vault doors — AA-D-600D and the QPL
itemListElement.name: L2-VAULT-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Federal vault doors are specified under federal specification AA-D-600D in three classes — Class 5-V, Class 5-A, and Class 5-B — and the manufacturers and model families the government has qualified are listed on Qualified Products List QPL-AA-D-600-12, Revision 12 of April 1, 2026. The three classes resist different attack types and are not a good-better-best ladder: Class 5-V is the full-resistance class (surreptitious, covert, and forced entry), Class 5-A drops the surreptitious requirement, and Class 5-B adds a ballistic requirement stated in the specification itself. Six manufacturers appear on Revision 12 of the QPL, each for named model families and classes — a maker's listing for one class says nothing about the others. A door's class belongs to the door as tested and listed; it is not a credential a mover or installer can hold.

itemListElement.headline: The lock is rated separately — UL 768 groups and FF-L-2740B
itemListElement.name: L2-VAULT-03
itemListElement.articleBody: A vault door's burglary rating covers the door; its lock is rated separately. UL 768 groups combination locks by manipulation resistance — Group 1 resists expert manipulation for 20 man-hours, Group 1R adds 20 man-hours of radiological attack resistance, Group 2M resists for 2 man-hours — and the standard states no hour figure for Group 2 at all. Federal Class 5 doors pair the door class with a lock meeting federal specification FF-L-2740B, whose locks resist manipulation, radiological attack, and emanations for 20 man-hours each and covert entry for 30 man-minutes; FF-L-2740B locks are for federal government and authorized-contractor use. Time locks are a separate device class again, standardized under UL 887. Any chart that prints an attack-hours figure for a plain Group 2 lock is publishing a number the standard does not contain.

itemListElement.headline: Vault door weights, openings, and installation planning
itemListElement.name: L2-VAULT-04
itemListElement.articleBody: A modern residential or commercial vault door is a four-figure load: manufacturer-stated weights for current production doors run from about 1,225 lbs to over 1,600 lbs, and the door must pass through a rough opening larger than the door itself, with clear swing room on the hinge side. Installation planning starts from the manufacturer's own figures: the door's stated weight, its rough-opening dimensions, its walk-through (clear) opening, and its swing direction. The path from the truck to the opening — thresholds, steps, floor spans — carries the same load as the final position, so floor structure is checked before the door moves, not after it arrives. Doors in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band sit in the weight range where structural relocation method (load spreading and floor-deflection analysis) is the deciding factor in a safe installation.

itemListElement.headline: Hoarding disorder prevalence and who it affects
itemListElement.name: L2-HOARD-01
itemListElement.articleBody: Hoarding disorder affects an estimated 2% to 6% of the population. A 2019 meta-analysis pooling 11 studies and 53,378 participants found a pooled prevalence of 2.5%, with earlier estimates ranging from roughly 1.5% to 6% by method. Symptoms appear almost three times more commonly in older adults than in younger adults, onset can occur by adolescence, and around 75% of people with hoarding disorder have a co-occurring mental-health condition, most commonly major depressive disorder. Rates are similar in men and women. For a cleanout provider the operative facts are that the condition is common, age-skewed, and usually entangled with grief, depression, or a triggering life event — which is why the client-led sort and a non-judgmental crew are operating requirements, not courtesies.

itemListElement.headline: Fire and life-safety risk in hoarded homes — the NFPA position
itemListElement.name: L2-HOARD-02
itemListElement.articleBody: NFPA’s guidance to the fire service states that fire departments are experiencing serious fires, injuries, and deaths as the result of compulsive hoarding behavior, and that the excessive accumulation of materials poses a significant threat to firefighters, residents, and neighbors. The mechanisms are specific: blocked exits prevent escape, obstructed exits and falling objects endanger responders, and excessive fire loading can lead to structural collapse, while hoarding makes fighting fires and searching for occupants far more difficult. NFPA publishes these as risk findings; it publishes no percentage of fire fatalities attributable to hoarding, and any source stating one is going beyond the evidence. This is the factual basis for treating code and fire-marshal deadlines in hoarding cases as emergencies.

itemListElement.headline: Code enforcement and the hoarding response process
itemListElement.name: L2-HOARD-03
itemListElement.articleBody: Hoarded properties usually surface through code enforcement. Martinsburg, WV enforces the 2015 International Property Maintenance Code: a confirmed violation draws a correction order with a deadline, and fines, liens, or condemnation stand behind it. The City of Alexandria, Virginia publishes a model hoarding-response procedure: document the conditions, involve code, fire, and adult protective services, and give written notice with deadlines before escalation. For the property owner the practical consequence is that the cleanout itself must be documentable — a written scope agreed before work begins and rooms photographed before and after are what a re-inspection accepts. There is no industry-wide standard for hoarding cleanups (the restoration trade press has noted the gap), so the written scope is the standard the buyer actually holds.

itemListElement.headline: Virginia: a tariff state — published rates are the legal price
itemListElement.name: L2-LOC-VA-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Every Virginia household goods carrier must file its tariffs — all rates and charges — with the Department at least thirty days before the effective date and make them available for public inspection (§46.2-2169). Charging or collecting more than the published tariff is unlawful (§46.2-2170), and the Department approves the rates and charges filed (§46.2-2155). Tariffs must separately state each accessorial service and its charge, including packing/unpacking per container or per hundredweight, and may establish an hourly labor charge for miscellaneous labor (§46.2-2173). itemListElement.headline: Virginia: written-estimate rules, and the bound (flat) estimate
itemListElement.name: L2-LOC-VA-03

itemListElement.headline: Virginia: weights are certified, observable, and re-weighable
itemListElement.name: L2-LOC-VA-05
itemListElement.articleBody: Where charges turn on weight, Virginia requires tare and gross weights taken on certified scales by a certified weighmaster, with the shipper entitled to observe the weighing; the net weight goes on the bill of lading (§46.2-2163). If no certified scale is available, a constructive weight of seven pounds per cubic foot of properly loaded van space may be used (§46.2-2164). Before delivery, the shipper may demand a reweigh, and the lower of the two net weights determines the charges (§46.2-2167). Section 46.2-2101(C) sets the minimum public financial responsibility for certificated household goods carriers at $750,000, and DMV application form OA 142 requires Form E (liability) and Form H (cargo) insurance filings for household-goods authority over 30 miles.
