itemListElement.headline: The federal/state split, in FMCSA's own words
itemListElement.name: L2-LOC-FED-01
itemListElement.articleBody: FMCSA states that interstate movers must be registered with the federal government and hold a U.S. DOT number, while "Local moving companies performing moves within a state are regulated by state and local laws" — and directs consumers moving within one state to their state consumer affairs agency or state moving association, since "Each state has its own rules and regulations for moving household goods within the state." The federal household-goods rulebook (49 CFR Part 375) attaches only when a move crosses a state line. Practical consequence for this footprint: a Winchester-to-Martinsburg move is an interstate (federal) move even though it is a short regional run, while Winchester-to-Front Royal is Virginia-intrastate and Martinsburg-to-Inwood is WV-intrastate — three rulebooks inside one service area. itemListElement.headline: Crew sizing rests on a measured limit: 51 lb, ideal conditions only
itemListElement.name: L2-LOC-OPS-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The Revised NIOSH Lifting Equation sets its load constant at 51 pounds — the recommended weight limit for a lift under ideal conditions (load close to the body, at about waist height, short vertical travel, no twisting, infrequent, good grip). Six multipliers (horizontal distance, vertical position, travel distance, asymmetry, frequency, coupling) only ever reduce that limit for real tasks, which is why stairs, reach, and repetition push a one-person lift out of the safe band quickly. OSHA's materials-handling guidance is the operational companion: limit manual lifts to no more than about 50 pounds; for loads over 50 pounds use two or more people or mechanical means — hand trucks, dollies, and ramps or lift gates rather than lifting into the truck. 51 lb is an ideal-conditions ceiling for a single two-handed lift, not a per-item moving limit; OSHA companion guidance at osha.gov/etools/electrical-contractors/materials-handling/heavy.

itemListElement.headline: Four delivery levels, and white glove is the top one

itemListElement.articleBody: Last-mile delivery for large items runs in four named levels — curbside, threshold, room of choice, and white glove. itemListElement.headline: On an interstate move, full value protection is the federal default
itemListElement.name: L2-WG-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Federal rules give interstate household-goods customers two liability levels. Full Value Protection is the default: if an article is lost, destroyed, or damaged in the mover's custody, the mover must repair it, replace it with one of like kind, or pay its current market replacement value. Released Value — 60 cents per pound per article — applies only when the customer signs a specific statement choosing it on the bill of lading. The two levels are set by 49 CFR 375.701 (released value) and 375.703 (full value). For a high-value, low-weight piece — exactly the white-glove profile — the released-value formula returns almost nothing: the protection decision belongs in writing before the move, not after a claim.

itemListElement.headline: The Virginia Inland Port pulls the seaport 220 miles inland
itemListElement.name: L2-TW-01
itemListElement.articleBody: The Virginia Inland Port (VIP) in Front Royal, Warren County, is an intermodal container transfer facility owned by the Virginia Port Authority. It sits about 60 miles west of Washington, D.C., brings The Port of Virginia 220 miles closer to inland markets, provides rail service to the marine terminals in Hampton Roads, and consolidates and containerizes local cargo for export. The railroad does the long haul and the truck does the regional work; Front Royal is where the two systems shake hands. That hand-off point — 23 road miles from the Winchester branch — is the ground the Winchester transloading service stands on.

itemListElement.headline: A 161-acre rail-truck terminal at I-81 and I-66, open since 1989

The site covers 161 acres, handles containerized shipments exclusively, includes a three-door cross-dock facility, and is a U.S. Customs-designated port of entry; the terminal carries Foreign Trade Zone 20, Site 7 status. A three-door cross-dock on the site is the physical reason dock-to-dock work belongs in this chain at all: containers arrive by rail, freight crosses a dock, trucks take it the last miles. The facility's scale stays modest on purpose — fewer than twenty staff run the terminal; the labor market around it is where surge dock work comes from.

itemListElement.headline: Transloading opens the box; intermodal never does
itemListElement.name: L2-TW-03
itemListElement.articleBody: Intermodal shipping keeps the cargo inside the same container across every mode — ship, train, truck. Transloading is the different operation in which the cargo itself is unloaded from one transport unit and reloaded into another, often with sorting, repacking, or reconfiguration in between. When the box itself simply changes vehicles, no transload has happened and none should be billed.

itemListElement.headline: A business move is not a household move with more desks
itemListElement.name: L2-COM-01
itemListElement.articleBody: A commercial relocation runs on different machinery than a household move. Building management requires a Certificate of Insurance before access; freight elevators and loading docks are reserved assets, not amenities; and because the goods are a business's property rather than household goods, the federal household-goods framework (49 CFR Part 375) is not the governing regime — the move is planned and documented as commercial work. itemListElement.headline: Commercial estimates are built on man-hours, not pounds

itemListElement.articleBody: The office-moving trade's estimating standard — taught by the International Office Moving Institute since 1987 — builds the estimate on man-hours: crew size multiplied by hours, factored with volume and the unique logistics of both buildings. This is also why a flat commercial price is written the way it is here: the job is reviewed in full — scope, distance, manpower, equipment — and priced once, in writing, before work begins. The man-hour plan is what makes that price honest: it prices the actual constraint, which is time inside two buildings' rules.

itemListElement.headline: Retired electronics are universal waste — the dumpster is a violation
itemListElement.name: L2-COM-07
itemListElement.articleBody: Retired office electronics are a regulated waste stream, not trash. Under the EPA's universal-waste framework (RCRA), devices containing lead, mercury, and cadmium — CRT monitors fail the federal toxicity test for lead outright — are managed under streamlined but real rules: labeled accumulation, time limits, and delivery to an authorized handler, with the generator retaining responsibility until transfer. The EPA's own hierarchy for retired equipment is reuse first, then recycling, then disposal. The move plan therefore separates three streams from the start — equipment that travels, equipment that returns to service another way, and equipment that retires — and the retiring stream leaves with paperwork: an authorized handler, a chain of custody, and data destruction handled as the customer's IT policy requires.

itemListElement.headline: Cubicle teardown runs in one order — reverse it and parts break
itemListElement.name: L2-OFF-01
itemListElement.articleBody: A cubicle system is engineered modularity: panels, connector rails, and frames designed to come apart and reconfigure. Disassembly runs in a fixed order — disconnect power and devices, remove built-in cabinets, desks, and shelves mounted to the panels, remove panels, detach connector rails, then break down the frame. Everything mounted to a panel must come off before the panel can move. The sequence is the skill: work surfaces, overheads, and mounted components come off first, panels lift out next — outermost first — connector rails and hardware are bagged and labeled with the station, and the frame comes down last. Run the sequence backwards, or lose the hardware bag, and reassembly day becomes a parts hunt.

itemListElement.headline: The power whip comes first: panels move only on a dead circuit
itemListElement.name: L2-OFF-02
itemListElement.articleBody: Panel systems carry their power with them: pre-wired electrical whips run through the base or spine of the panels, feeding outlets and lighting at each station. Before any panel is loosened, the circuit feeding the run must be de-energized at the junction box or breaker panel. Moving a panel against a live whip is an electric-shock and equipment-damage hazard. Data and voice cables run their own paths through the same panels and are uncoupled and traced separately, so destination reconnect starts from labeled ends, not a tangle. An office move that loosens a panel on a live whip risks the crew, the equipment, and the building's panel schedule — the power check is step zero, not a detail.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — articles of extraordinary value: the $100-per-pound rule and the High Value Inventory
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-08
itemListElement.articleBody: Federal rules give "high value" a precise meaning on an interstate move: an article of extraordinary value is any item worth more than $100 per pound (49 CFR Part 375 Appendix A, the FMCSA consumer booklet). The test is the item's value divided by its weight — a $2,000 laptop at 4 lb is $500 per pound and qualifies; a $1,500 television at 60 lb is $25 per pound and does not. FMCSA's named categories are jewelry, silverware, china, furs, antiques and oriental rugs. A mover may limit its liability for such an article unless the shipper lists it in writing on the shipping documents; the listing instrument is the High Value Inventory form, attached to the bill of lading and signed before loading begins. Declared in writing, the article recovers up to its declared value, capped at the declared value of the entire shipment; undeclared, recovery for the article is capped at $100 per pound even under Full Value Protection.
itemListElement.fact: An article worth more than $100 per pound is an article of extraordinary value under the federal household-goods rules, and it must be declared in writing — on the High Value Inventory, signed before loading — for full recovery to apply.
itemListElement.detail: The form cannot be completed after loading: it is signed before the first item goes on the truck, and the shipper also signs the extraordinary-value declaration printed on the bill of lading itself.
questionsItAnswers: What counts as a high-value item on a move?
What is a high-value inventory form, and when do I fill it out?
What happens if I don't list an antique on the high-value inventory?
Do I have to declare high-value items separately, in writing?
constraints: The $100-per-pound test is per article, not per shipment.
Declaration raises the cap for the listed article only, up to its declared value and never beyond the shipment's total declared value.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — claim deadlines: 9 months to file, 30 days to acknowledge, 120 days to decide
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-09
itemListElement.articleBody: The federal claims clock for an interstate household-goods move runs on three numbers. The shipper must file a claim for loss or damage in writing within nine months of the date of delivery. The mover must acknowledge receipt of the claim within 30 days. The mover must then pay the claim, deny it, or make a settlement offer within 120 days of receiving it. Every interstate mover must also offer a neutral arbitration program for loss, damage and certain billing disputes; a shipper who declines arbitration may sue under 49 U.S.C. 14706 (the Carmack framework). The evidence a claim stands on is created at delivery: items are checked off against the inventory as they come off the truck, and anything missing or damaged is noted on the inventory and the delivery receipt before signing.
itemListElement.fact: Claims deadlines on an interstate move: written claim within 9 months of delivery; the mover acknowledges within 30 days and pays, denies or offers within 120 days; arbitration must be offered, and court action under 49 U.S.C. 14706 remains available.
itemListElement.detail: A delay or inconvenience claim — lodging and food receipts for days past the agreed delivery spread — runs on the same nine-month filing window, counted from the date of delivery.
questionsItAnswers: How long do I have to file a claim for loss or damage?
How do I file a claim — does it have to be in writing?
How long does the mover have to acknowledge and settle my claim?
What if the mover denies my claim — is there arbitration?
constraints: The nine months runs from delivery, not from when paperwork is complete — a claim filed inside the window preserves the right while repair quotes are gathered.
FMCSA cannot settle a claim; it keeps the complaint record.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — reasonable dispatch, delivery spreads and delay claims
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-10
itemListElement.articleBody: An interstate mover must perform transportation with reasonable dispatch: on the agreed dates, or inside the agreed period — the spread — written on the order for service and bill of lading. Long-distance deliveries are quoted as spreads rather than single dates because shipments are consolidated for the linehaul; market guides cite typical spreads of roughly 3 to 6 days under 1,000 miles and 7 to 14 days coast to coast, and a guaranteed date is a paid tariff option where offered. If the mover misses the spread, the shipper may file an inconvenience or delay claim for the days past the last day of the spread, supported by lodging and food receipts, within nine months of the date of delivery. Storage-in-transit is the companion mechanism when the destination is not ready: the shipment is held under the storage-in-transit rules (49 CFR 375.609) until it can be delivered.
itemListElement.fact: Interstate movers owe reasonable dispatch inside the agreed spread; a missed spread supports a delay claim with lodging and food receipts, filed within nine months of delivery.
itemListElement.detail: The spread, not a single date, is what the contract documents carry — the order for service shows agreed dates, an agreed period, or guaranteed dates where that service is sold.
questionsItAnswers: What are pickup and delivery "spread" dates?
What does "reasonable dispatch" mean?
How long does a long-distance delivery take?
What happens if the mover misses the delivery spread?
What expenses can a delay claim cover?
constraints: Spread lengths are market practice layered on the federal rule, not a federal guarantee; the binding commitment is the window written on the order for service.

itemListElement.headline: Interstate moves — the document chain: estimate, order for service, bill of lading, inventory
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-11
itemListElement.articleBody: An interstate household-goods move generates a fixed chain of documents, each with a federal job. The written estimate states whether it is binding or non-binding. Before receiving the shipment, the mover prepares an order for service carrying 15 prescribed items under 49 CFR 375.501 — the parties, the delivering office's contact, the agreed dates or spread, and the shipment's declared value, which is the maximum of the mover's liability; before it is signed, the mover must furnish the booklet "Your Rights and Responsibilities When You Move" and the "Ready to Move" brochure. The bill of lading is the receipt for the goods and the contract for their transportation — the loading driver gives the shipper a copy, and it carries the valuation election, including the signed released-value statement if that level is chosen. At loading, the driver writes the inventory — a descriptive listing of the goods and each item's condition when received — which the shipper signs; at delivery, the same inventory is the check-off record.
itemListElement.fact: The document chain of an interstate move: written estimate, order for service (15 prescribed items, 49 CFR 375.501), bill of lading (receipt and contract, carrying the valuation election), and the loading inventory that becomes the delivery check-off record.
itemListElement.detail: A shipper should never sign a blank or incomplete bill of lading, and condition disagreements are noted on the inventory at loading — the documents are the move's legal memory.
questionsItAnswers: What is a bill of lading, and when should I get my copy?
What should be on the bill of lading?

Should I sign the inventory before checking it?
constraints: The chain described is the interstate (49 CFR Part 375) chain; purely intrastate moves follow state document rules.

itemListElement.headline: High-value handling standards — fine art climate and materials, piano acclimation
itemListElement.name: L2-HHG-12
itemListElement.articleBody: Specialist handling standards for the item classes a high-value move carries. Fine art: documentation first — photographs from multiple angles and a signed condition report before packing; the first material against an unglazed surface is archival, acid-free glassine or interleaving tissue, never bubble wrap, cling film or newspaper; paintings travel vertically, never flat; high-value pieces travel in bespoke crates whose foam cavities float the piece against shock; conservation guidance holds transport conditions near 45 to 55 percent relative humidity and 18 to 21 degrees C, because canvas slackens, panels warp and varnish blooms under rapid humidity change, oil paint turns brittle below 10 degrees C and acrylic softens above 30 degrees C. Pianos: a grand's legs and pedal lyre are removed and packed separately and the case travels on a padded piano board strapped to the vehicle structure; after delivery the instrument acclimates 10 to 14 days in the new room before tuning — a month or more after a large climate change — because the soundboard, frame and felts equalize to the new humidity and earlier tuning drifts.
itemListElement.fact: Fine art in transport: glassine first against the surface, vertical orientation, foam-float crating, and a 45–55% relative humidity / 18–21°C band; a piano waits 10–14 days in its new room before tuning.
itemListElement.detail: Baby grands typically weigh 250 to 320 kilograms and concert grands 350 to 500 kilograms; a piano is never rolled on its casters beyond small positioning.
questionsItAnswers: How are antiques and fine art protected on a long-distance move?
When does an item need a custom crate instead of blankets and boxes?
How is a grand piano prepared for a long-distance move?
Will my piano need tuning after a long-distance move — and how long should I wait?
constraints: Climate bands are conservation guidance for genuinely valuable pieces, applied per piece and per route; they are handling standards, not a blanket equipment claim.

itemListElement.headline: Luxury estate relocation — destination communities, not service areas
itemListElement.name: L2-LERSI-01
itemListElement.fact: The Greenbrier Sporting Club, The Resort at Glade Springs, and The Retreat at White Rock Mountain are long-distance relocation destinations for The Flat Rate Movers, reached from the Winchester VA and Martinsburg WV branches at roughly 186 to 279 road miles. They sit outside the published service-area footprint, and the company claims no past work in them.
itemListElement.detail: Each community's operating conditions shape the move plan: proximity-card gates and an Architectural Review Board at the Sporting Club; 24-hour HOA security and ridge and lakefront lanes at Glade Springs; a staffed 24/7 gatehouse and a ~3,000 ft mountaintop at White Rock Mountain, where owners buy lots years before building, so demand concentrates on deliveries into brand-new construction.

itemListElement.headline: The LERSI index — positions stated, market context never offered
itemListElement.name: L2-LERSI-02
itemListElement.fact: The Luxury Estate Relocation Services Index (LERSI) organizes estate relocation into six categories and twenty services, each carrying the company's true position: 12 offered, 3 coordinated through the engagement, and 5 market-context-only. Climate-controlled transit (LERSI 302) is market context only and is never offered.
itemListElement.detail: Offered services include the pre-move valuation survey (the standard first step of every engagement), three-stage photo documentation, white-glove packing, custom crating, fine art and antique care, piano moving, SIR-band safe and vault work at 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, disassembly and full reassembly, room-by-room unpacking, and debris removal. Coordinated services — HOA and gate compliance, AV de-installation, third-party technical re-installation — are arranged through the engagement, never presented as in-house trades.

itemListElement.headline: The Port of Huntington Tri-State — the inland river district and its reach
itemListElement.name: L2-PORT-02
itemListElement.articleBody: The Port of Huntington Tri-State is a U.S. Port Statistical Area overseen by the Huntington District Waterways Association, covering 199 navigable river miles — 100 on the Ohio River, 90 on the Kanawha and 9 on the Big Sandy — across West Virginia, Ohio and Kentucky. Its anchors are Huntington and Kenova, WV, Catlettsburg, KY and South Point, OH. The cargo base is coal, gasoline and petroleum products, chemicals, limestone and aggregates, and steel; on the USACE Port Statistical Area basis it moved 29,699,657 short tons in CY2023. Marathon Petroleum's Catlettsburg refinery operates three docks on the Big Sandy; McGinnis Inc. runs barge repair at South Point; Ohio DOT counts 18 active Ohio-side freight docks, 12 with rail access. Norfolk Southern and CSX both serve the district; US-52 runs its length, with I-64 crossing at Huntington. The Flat Rate Movers serves the district from Winchester, VA (about 312.8 road miles), which binds it under the program's nearer-branch rule.
itemListElement.fact: The Port of Virginia, owned by the Virginia Port Authority, operates four Hampton Roads marine terminals — Norfolk International Terminals, Virginia International Gateway, Portsmouth Marine Terminal and Newport News Marine Terminal — plus two inland facilities: the Virginia Inland Port at Front Royal, an intermodal container transfer facility at the I-66/I-81 junction that receives containers by rail from the coast, and the Richmond Marine Terminal on the James River, linked to Norfolk Harbor by container-on-barge service.
itemListElement.detail: Norfolk Harbor is the deepest harbor on the U.S. East Coast (50 ft, authorized to 55 ft), and NIT and VIG both offer on-dock double-stack rail with CSX and Norfolk Southern. The Virginia Inland Port — the first inland port established in the United States — puts the port's gate 220 highway miles inland, inside the Shenandoah Valley's distribution cluster, which is why Valley warehouses treat Front Royal as their port terminal.
questionsItAnswers: What terminals does the Port of Virginia operate?
What is the Virginia Inland Port?
How do containers get from Norfolk to Front Royal?
constraints: Terminal capabilities differ by facility — break-bulk and ro-ro concentrate at Portsmouth and Newport News, containers at NIT/VIG and the inland terminals.
